item.title: Annual house price inflation slowest since 2023
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New data from Lloyds Banking Group suggests the UK housing market is experiencing its slowest annual price growth since 2023, with property values remaining largely static in recent months. The figures indicate that higher mortgage rates and subdued buyer activity are continuing to influence market conditions across most regions.

Market slowdown continues

The latest house price index reveals annual inflation has dipped to its lowest level in over a year, with month-on-month changes showing minimal movement. Several factors appear to be contributing to this trend:

  • Elevated mortgage rates making affordability challenging for many buyers
  • Reduced transaction volumes compared to previous years
  • Ongoing economic uncertainty affecting buyer confidence

Whilst prices aren't falling significantly in most areas, the data suggests the market has entered a period of relative stability after the more volatile conditions seen during and immediately after the pandemic.

Regional variations persist

As with previous slowdowns, the impact isn't uniform across the country. Some regions continue to record modest price growth, while others show slight declines. The Lloyds report indicates:

  • London and the South East are seeing the most pronounced slowdown
  • More affordable northern regions are demonstrating greater resilience
  • Certain property types, particularly family homes, are maintaining values better than flats

Prospective buyers and homeowners considering a move might find it helpful to research local market conditions thoroughly, as national averages can mask significant regional differences.

With interest rates remaining higher than the ultra-low levels seen in recent years, the housing market appears to be adjusting to a new normal. Those monitoring the situation may wish to keep an eye on upcoming economic indicators and Bank of England announcements for signs of future direction.

item.title: £4.1 bn cost of tenancy fraud
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent analysis has shed light on the growing issue of tenancy fraud within the UK’s private rented sector, revealing a staggering £4.1 billion cost to landlords and property investors. The findings highlight not only the financial impact but also the increasing sophistication of fraudulent applications, posing significant challenges for the industry.

The Rising Threat of Tenancy Fraud

Tenancy fraud occurs when individuals provide false information or documentation to secure rental properties. This can range from fabricated income details to falsified references or identity documents. With advancements in technology, fraudsters are becoming more adept at creating convincing forgeries, making it harder for landlords and letting agents to detect dishonest applications.

This trend has led to substantial financial losses for property owners, who may face unpaid rent, property damage, or lengthy legal battles to evict fraudulent tenants. The £4.1 billion figure underscores the scale of the problem, emphasising the need for greater vigilance and improved verification processes within the sector.

How Fraud Impacts the Rental Market

The repercussions of tenancy fraud extend beyond financial losses. Landlords may become more cautious when selecting tenants, potentially leading to longer void periods or stricter application criteria. This could make it more challenging for genuine renters, particularly those with complex financial situations, to secure housing.

Additionally, the rising cost of fraud may contribute to higher rental prices, as landlords seek to offset their losses. This creates a ripple effect across the market, impacting affordability for tenants and increasing pressure on an already strained rental sector.

Steps to Combat Tenancy Fraud

To tackle this issue, landlords and letting agents might consider implementing more robust tenant verification processes. This could include:

  • Conducting thorough background checks, including credit history and employment verification.
  • Utilising digital tools to verify identity documents and detect forgeries.
  • Requesting references from previous landlords or employers.
  • Working with reputable referencing agencies to ensure accuracy.

Technology can play a key role in reducing fraud, with platforms offering enhanced verification services becoming increasingly accessible. Investing in these tools could help landlords protect their properties and minimise risks.

The £4.1 billion cost of tenancy fraud highlights the urgent need for action within the private rented sector. By adopting stronger verification measures and leveraging technology, landlords and agents can better safeguard their investments and create a more secure rental market for all parties involved.

item.title: Resi construction starts down 25% in Q2
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK housing market has faced significant challenges in recent months, with new data revealing a sharp decline in residential construction starts during the second quarter of the year. According to industry reports, private housing activity has dropped by 25% compared to the previous quarter, highlighting the impact of ongoing economic and political uncertainty on the property sector.

Economic and Political Factors Impacting Construction

The slowdown in residential construction starts can be attributed to a combination of factors, including rising inflation, higher interest rates, and broader economic instability. These conditions have led to increased caution among developers and investors, many of whom are delaying new projects until the outlook becomes clearer. Additionally, political uncertainty, particularly surrounding government policies and planning reforms, has further contributed to the hesitation in committing to new developments.

Construction firms are also grappling with rising costs, including materials and labour, which have squeezed profit margins and made new projects less financially viable. This has led to a more conservative approach in the industry, with many developers focusing on completing existing projects rather than starting new ones.

Implications for the Housing Market

The decline in residential construction starts could have significant implications for the UK housing market. With fewer new homes being built, the already constrained supply of properties is likely to worsen, potentially driving up house prices and rents in the long term. This could exacerbate the affordability crisis, particularly for first-time buyers and those on lower incomes.

For homeowners and property investors, the slowdown in construction activity may also limit opportunities for new developments or extensions. However, it could also create a more competitive market for existing properties, particularly in high-demand areas.

Whilst the current situation presents challenges, some industry experts suggest that the slowdown may be temporary. As economic conditions stabilise and clarity emerges on key policy issues, construction activity could rebound. In the meantime, borrowers may wish to explore their options carefully, particularly when it comes to financing property purchases or renovations.

As the UK housing market navigates this period of uncertainty, staying informed about trends and developments will be crucial for homeowners, buyers, and investors alike.

item.title: Rely drives growth for OSB Group buy-to-let
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The OSB Group has reported robust growth in its buy-to-let mortgage lending, driven primarily by its specialist brand Rely. Increased refinancing activity and growing demand for longer-term fixed rate deals have contributed to this strong performance in the specialist lending market.

Refinancing fuels buy-to-let lending momentum

Many landlords appear to be reassessing their mortgage arrangements amidst ongoing economic uncertainty. The OSB Group's latest figures suggest a notable uptick in refinancing applications as property investors seek more favourable terms. Borrowers might consider reviewing their existing buy-to-let mortgages, particularly if they're approaching the end of their current fixed or tracker rate periods.

The trend reflects broader market movements where homeowners and investors alike are exploring options to secure stable repayment costs. Specialist lenders like those within the OSB Group often cater to landlords with complex financial circumstances, offering tailored solutions that high street banks may not provide.

Longer fixed rate deals gain traction

Alongside refinancing activity, there's growing interest in longer-term fixed rate mortgages amongst buy-to-let investors. Five-year fixes in particular have seen increased popularity as landlords look to hedge against potential future base rate rises. The stability offered by these products could prove particularly valuable for those managing multiple properties or operating within tighter budgets.

Mortgage providers have responded to this demand by expanding their product ranges, with some specialist lenders now offering fixed terms extending up to seven years. Whilst longer fixes typically come with slightly higher rates, the certainty they provide may outweigh the marginally increased costs for many property investors.

With the buy-to-let market continuing to evolve, keeping abreast of mortgage trends remains crucial for landlords. Those reviewing their financing options may wish to explore both refinancing opportunities and the expanding range of fixed term products available in today's specialist lending market.

item.title: Algarve tops overseas searches
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research highlights Portugal's Algarve region as the most sought-after overseas property destination for British buyers, according to the latest data from Rightmove. The sunny southern coastline continues to outrank other international locations, offering a combination of year-round sunshine, golf courses and relatively affordable property prices compared to other European hotspots.

What makes the Algarve appealing?

The Algarve's enduring popularity stems from several key factors that resonate with UK property hunters. The region boasts over 300 days of sunshine annually, making it particularly attractive for those seeking warmer climates. Its well-established expat community and English-speaking services provide an easier transition for British buyers.

Property types in the area range from coastal apartments to traditional villas, with price points to suit various budgets. Whilst prime waterfront locations command premium prices, more affordable options can be found slightly inland. The region's developed infrastructure, including international schools and healthcare facilities, adds to its practical appeal for those considering relocation.

Other popular destinations for British buyers

Beyond Portugal, Rightmove's data reveals several other locations attracting significant interest from UK-based property seekers:

  • Spain's Costa del Sol remains a firm favourite, particularly for its familiar culture and established British communities
  • France continues to draw buyers with its rural charm and proximity to the UK
  • Italy's Tuscany region appeals to those seeking picturesque countryside and cultural heritage
  • Florida in the US maintains its position as a top long-haul destination for British investors

When considering overseas property purchases, prospective buyers might want to research local property laws, tax implications and currency exchange factors. Consulting with independent financial advisers and legal experts familiar with the target country's regulations could help avoid potential pitfalls.

Whilst international property markets offer exciting opportunities, thorough research and professional guidance remain essential for making informed decisions. The Algarve's current popularity reflects ongoing trends in British buyers' preferences, but individual circumstances and requirements should always guide any overseas property investment.

item.title: New tool gives agents early insight into sellers’ price expectations
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Estate agents now have access to fresh insights into homeowners' pricing expectations, thanks to a new tool launched by ValPal. The feature allows potential sellers to share their own valuation estimates alongside automated property appraisals, helping bridge the gap between data-driven estimates and sellers' personal perspectives.

How the Valuation Feedback Tool Works

After receiving an initial automated property valuation online, homeowners can adjust a slider to indicate their own price expectations. They may also leave comments highlighting unique features they believe add value – from proximity to transport links to home improvements that wouldn't appear in standard data sets. This feedback is immediately shared with estate agents alongside the valuation enquiry.

Craig Vile of ValPal Network explains: "Homeowners often feel automated systems miss their property's unique qualities – whether that's a desirable location, recent extensions, or simply years of careful maintenance. This tool gives them a voice in the valuation process from the outset."

Benefits for Agents and Sellers Alike

The innovation aims to foster more transparent conversations between agents and potential sellers by:

  • Providing immediate insight into sellers' pricing expectations
  • Highlighting property features that may not appear in valuation algorithms
  • Helping agents prepare more tailored market appraisals
  • Reducing potential mismatches in price expectations early in the process

Vile emphasises that while homeowners' input provides valuable context, professional judgement remains paramount: "Technology analyses data, homeowners know their properties intimately, and agents bring market expertise. Combining these elements helps establish appropriate asking prices from day one."

Currently available to all ValPal users at no extra cost, the tool is designed to complement – not replace – traditional valuation methods. For homeowners considering selling, it represents an opportunity to ensure their property's unique qualities are factored into initial discussions about its market value.

item.title: Housing tech firms combine AI and human support for out-of-hours calls
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Two UK property technology firms have joined forces to streamline out-of-hours emergency repairs and maintenance requests for housing providers and facilities management teams. Askporter and PropCall’s new partnership integrates artificial intelligence with round-the-clock human support, aiming to improve response times and reduce unnecessary costs.

AI and human collaboration for emergency responses

The hybrid system uses Askporter’s automated triage platform to assess incoming enquiries via WhatsApp, SMS, email and web channels. Routine maintenance requests are filtered through standard daytime processes, while urgent cases outside working hours are escalated to PropCall’s 24/7 call handlers. These agents can authorise emergency repairs up to £500 in value, based on pre-agreed client guidelines.

Till Eichenauer, Askporter’s chief executive, highlighted the current challenges: "Many property teams rely on expensive tradesperson rotas that often go unused, or divert all calls to voicemail where genuine emergencies get lost among routine queries. This new solution aims to meet rising expectations around rapid hazard responses, particularly in light of Awaab’s Law."

Benefits for housing providers and residents

The integrated service offers several advantages for property managers and occupants alike. By automatically categorising enquiries, the system reduces the volume of non-urgent cases reaching out-of-hours teams. All cases are digitally recorded, creating a continuous audit trail between overnight and daytime operations.

For housing teams, this means starting each day with prioritised case notes rather than manually sifting through overnight communications. Josh Kinniburgh of PropCall explained: "Our combination of AI triage and human expertise ensures residents speak to someone who understands their situation, while preventing minor issues from escalating into costly problems over weekends."

The partnership comes as social housing providers face increasing pressure to improve maintenance response times. With this new system, a water leak reported late on Friday could be addressed immediately rather than causing extensive damage by Monday morning – potentially saving thousands in repair costs while improving tenant satisfaction.

As property technology continues to evolve, such integrations between automation and human oversight may become increasingly valuable for housing providers balancing efficiency with quality service.

item.title: UK housing market ‘not broken but barely breathing’
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK housing market has shown minimal growth in recent months, with house prices remaining largely stagnant, according to the latest Lloyds House Price Index. The data reveals that annual house price growth has slowed to just 0.1%, marking the weakest rate since November 2023. The average property price in July stood at £299,253, a marginal decline of £143 from June’s figure of £299,396. This stagnation has sparked discussions about the current state of the market and its future trajectory.

A Market in Suspended Animation

Industry experts describe the housing market as being in a state of “suspended animation,” with prices neither falling sharply nor rising significantly. Anthony Codling, managing director of equity research at RBC Capital Markets, likened the market to being “barely breathing.” He noted that affordability constraints and persistently high mortgage rates have created a ceiling on buyer demand. Whilst geopolitical tensions have contributed to lenders nudging rates back up, this has further dampened market activity.

Transaction volumes remain well below levels seen a year ago, and surveys from the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) continue to reflect subdued demand. Codling highlighted that whilst stable prices are preferable to declines, the lack of volume recovery poses challenges for housebuilders, making it difficult to sustain earnings momentum.

Affordability Challenges and Regional Variations

Nathan Emerson, CEO of Propertymark, acknowledged the affordability challenges faced by both existing homeowners and first-time buyers in 2026. He emphasised that buying a home is a long-term commitment and that market fluctuations are influenced by broader economic and global factors. Emerson pointed to steady interest rates and a recent unexpected fall in inflation as potential signs of improving conditions, which could bolster buyer confidence in the coming months.

However, lower mortgage applications and reduced lending over the previous quarter are expected to continue impacting market activity. Emerson also noted that economic recovery could vary by region, and changing political priorities may lead to differing housing policies across the UK nations.

For those considering entering the market or remortgaging, it could be worth keeping a close eye on interest rate trends and regional developments. Homeowners may wish to explore their options carefully, particularly in light of the current affordability pressures.

In summary, whilst the UK housing market is not in crisis, it remains in a delicate state. Affordability challenges, mortgage rate fluctuations, and regional variations continue to shape the market’s trajectory. Borrowers might consider seeking professional advice to navigate these uncertain conditions effectively.

item.title: House price growth slows to weakest rate since 2023
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

UK house price growth has slowed to its weakest annual rate since late 2023, according to the latest Lloyds House Price Index. Property values remained essentially flat in July, with just a 0.1% year-on-year increase and no monthly change from June's figures. The average home now costs £299,253 – marginally lower than June's figure of £299,396.

Market stability amid affordability challenges

Lloyds' data reveals remarkable price stability over the past two years, with values just 0.5% higher than in November 2024. Amanda Bryden, head of mortgages at Lloyds, noted that affordability pressures continue to challenge buyers whilst mortgage rates have begun creeping up again after their summer easing. Recent geopolitical tensions in the Middle East have contributed to this upward trend in borrowing costs.

The market shows clear sensitivity to interest rate movements, with mortgage approvals and completed transactions seeing a modest June recovery following May's sharper decline. Bryden observed that whilst housing demand remains steady overall, market activity continues reacting swiftly to any changes in mortgage pricing.

Regional variations in price performance

item.title: London renters need £74,520 salary for average property
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Renting in London has become increasingly unaffordable, with tenants now needing an annual salary of £74,520 to secure the average-priced property, according to recent data from Propertymark. This represents a 6.4% increase from last year's £70,050 threshold, while average monthly rents have risen 4.2% to £2,484. The figures highlight growing affordability challenges in the capital's rental market.

Regional Rental Variations

While London dominates with the highest costs, regional markets show diverse trends. The North West recorded the second-largest monthly rent increase at 1.9%, pushing the required salary to £33,930. Meanwhile, Wales bucked the trend with rents falling 0.9% to £1,000 per month, reducing the necessary income to £30,000.

Other regions experienced mixed movements:

  • Rises in the West Midlands (1.7%), South East (0.8%) and Scotland (0.2%)
  • Declines in the East Midlands (-1.1%), North East (-0.9%) and South West (-0.7%)
  • Minor drops in Eastern England (-0.2%) and Yorkshire & Humberside (-0.1%)

Market Dynamics and Outlook

Kim Lidbury of ARLA Propertymark notes that rental growth, whilst slowing compared to previous years, remains elevated due to chronic supply shortages. "Demand continues to significantly outstrip available properties," she explains, "meaning rents stay historically high despite more moderate increases."

The data suggests tenants hoping for substantial rent reductions may face disappointment without policy changes to boost housing supply. Lidbury emphasises that meaningful affordability improvements would require both increased stock and measures to support landlord investment in the private rental sector.

For renters navigating these challenging conditions, thorough budgeting and early preparation for referencing checks could prove valuable when searching for properties. Those considering a move might benefit from researching local market trends, as rental pressures vary considerably between regions.

item.title: Landlord database ‘must not add new burden to every instruction’
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The government’s forthcoming landlord database could create unnecessary administrative burdens for letting agents unless its design aligns with existing industry practices, according to Propertymark. The professional body has urged policymakers to ensure the Private Rented Sector Database integrates smoothly with current systems to avoid duplicating work for property professionals.

Streamlining the registration process

Propertymark supports the concept of a national landlord register but emphasises the importance of practical implementation. The trade body suggests the database should connect directly with agency software and utilise information already provided through local licensing schemes. Without this integration, letting agents may face significant additional workloads, including manual data entry, verification checks and ongoing monitoring of registration statuses.

Whilst landlords bear primary responsibility for registration, agents cannot treat this as purely their clients’ concern. Under the Renters’ Rights Act 2025, marketing an unregistered property becomes illegal – with liability extending to the advertiser. This means agents will need to incorporate registration checks into their standard property onboarding processes.

Potential operational impacts

The new system, scheduled for regional rollout from late 2026, will require both landlords and properties to be registered before marketing can commence. Agents may need to:

  • Verify registration status before listing properties
  • Include unique identifiers in all advertisements
  • Maintain records of registration details
  • Confirm ongoing compliance throughout tenancies

Propertymark is currently gathering evidence from members about the potential operational impacts, including estimated staff hours for compliance, system upgrade costs and the proportion of properties likely to be affected. The body has warned against implementing a system that requires excessive manual intervention, which could drive up costs for both agents and landlords.

Penalties for non-compliance could reach £7,000 for initial breaches, escalating to £40,000 or criminal prosecution for repeated offences. With such significant consequences, many agents may feel compelled to implement rigorous internal checks, potentially adding time and cost to every instruction.

As the database development continues, industry voices are calling for a solution that enhances transparency without creating unnecessary bureaucracy. The coming months will prove crucial in shaping a system that balances regulatory objectives with practical operation for the private rented sector.

item.title: Mortgage fraud rise is ‘worrying trend’ for property market
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent data has revealed a concerning uptick in mortgage fraud across the UK, with cases rising in every reported category. According to the latest figures from Cifas, the first half of 2026 saw significant increases in identity fraud, false applications, account takeovers, and misuse of facility cases linked to mortgages. This trend has raised alarms within the property market, prompting calls for enhanced verification measures to safeguard consumers and lenders alike.

Key Areas of Mortgage Fraud Growth

One of the most notable increases has been in mortgage application identity fraud, which surged by 36% compared to the same period in 2025. False mortgage applications also rose by 4%, reaching 691 cases and representing the largest category by volume. Account takeover cases, although relatively small in number, saw a dramatic jump from just one incident in the first half of 2025 to 27 in the same period this year. Additionally, misuse of facility cases, which had been declining overall, bucked the trend within the mortgage sector, increasing from three to nine incidents.

Experts have highlighted the growing sophistication of fraudsters, who are increasingly using stolen or fake identities as well as compromised accounts to target lenders, intermediaries, and consumers. This shift underscores the limitations of relying solely on traditional document checks and emphasises the need for more robust, digital verification solutions.

The Importance of Enhanced Security Measures

The rise in mortgage fraud has significant implications for the property market. Beyond the financial risks to lenders, fraud poses a threat to buyers, sellers, and the integrity of the entire homebuying process. As fraud volumes continue to climb, stakeholders are being urged to invest in advanced verification technologies to ensure a secure and efficient experience for all parties involved.

David Jones, chief executive of Click2Check, commented on the findings, stating, “The latest Cifas fraud figures highlight a worrying trend for the property market, with mortgage fraud increasing across every category. Preventing fraud is about more than protecting lenders – it’s about safeguarding buyers, sellers, and the integrity of the entire transaction.”

As fraudsters adapt their tactics, the property sector must respond with equally innovative solutions. Digital verification tools, such as biometric checks and real-time identity validation, are becoming essential components of a secure mortgage process. These measures not only help to detect and prevent fraud but also streamline the homebuying journey for legitimate applicants.

With overall fraud cases reaching a record high in the first six months of 2026, the need for vigilance and proactive measures has never been greater. By prioritising security and adopting cutting-edge verification technologies, the property market can better protect itself against the evolving threat of mortgage fraud.

item.title: The Property Flipper’s Guide to Site Clearance and Quick Skip Hire
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Property flipping can be an attractive way to generate returns, but the process often involves more groundwork than the glossy 'after' photos suggest. One frequently overlooked aspect is site clearance – the unglamorous but essential first step that can make or break a project's budget and timeline.

The Hidden Costs of Site Clearance

Many property investors focus on the visible transformations – new kitchens, landscaped gardens or modernised interiors. However, the initial strip-out phase often presents unexpected challenges. Older properties may contain outdated materials requiring specialist disposal, while probate homes sometimes come with decades of accumulated belongings. Underestimating clearance requirements can lead to:

  • Project delays from extended skip hire periods
  • Budget overruns due to additional waste removal
  • Hidden costs like hazardous material disposal
  • Storage fees for items awaiting clearance

Planning an Efficient Clearance Strategy

Experienced flippers typically develop systematic approaches to site clearance. Some key considerations include:

  • Waste audits: Assessing the volume and type of materials needing removal before ordering skips
  • Permit checks: Verifying local council regulations for skip placement and waste disposal
  • Recycling opportunities: Identifying salvageable materials that could be sold or donated
  • Contingency planning: Allocating extra budget and time for unexpected clearance requirements

For those new to property renovation, consulting with experienced clearance specialists might prove valuable. Many firms offer fixed-price quotes based on property size and condition, helping investors avoid unpredictable costs.

While site clearance lacks the visual appeal of later renovation stages, proper planning at this phase often determines a project's overall success. By factoring in realistic timelines and budgets for this essential first step, property investors can create more accurate project plans and protect their profit margins.

item.title: London asking rents accelerate despite falling demand
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

London’s rental market continues to defy expectations, with advertised rents rising sharply despite a noticeable drop in tenant demand. According to recent data from online agency Hello Neighbour, asking rents in the capital increased by 8.7% in July compared to the same month last year. This marks an acceleration from the 6.4% annual rise recorded in June. However, this upward trend in rental prices coincides with a decline in tenant enquiries, which fell to an average of 34 per property in July, down from 43 in June and significantly lower than the 93 enquiries recorded in July 2023.

Rising Rents Amid Falling Demand

The latest figures highlight a growing trend of rental prices climbing whilst tenant demand weakens. Hello Neighbour attributes this to a combination of reduced net migration and ongoing affordability pressures faced by renters. Despite the drop in demand, rental supply has remained stable, contributing to the upward pressure on prices. This suggests that landlords are feeling confident in their ability to secure higher rents, even as fewer tenants compete for available properties.

Another notable development is the widening gap between advertised rents and the rents landlords ultimately achieve. In July, this gap increased to 2.7 percentage points, up from 1.4 in June. This trend may be linked to recent changes introduced by the Renters’ Rights Act, which restricts landlords from accepting offers above the advertised rent and imposes tighter controls on rent increases during tenancies. As a result, landlords may be incentivised to set higher initial asking prices, knowing they cannot adjust rents as easily once a tenancy begins.

The Impact of Legislative Changes

The Renters’ Rights Act, which came into effect earlier this year, appears to be reshaping landlord behaviour in the London rental market. By limiting landlords’ ability to negotiate higher rents after a property is advertised, the legislation has encouraged a more cautious approach to pricing. Landlords may now be advertising properties at higher initial rents to safeguard against potential income restrictions during the tenancy. This could explain the growing disparity between asking rents and the rents landlords ultimately achieve.

Looking ahead, Hello Neighbour predicts that rental growth is likely to persist for the remainder of the year. The agency suggests that tenant demand may stabilise as the effects of reduced net migration begin to ease. Additionally, landlords’ responses to the Renters’ Rights Act are expected to become more established in the coming months, potentially leading to further adjustments in rental pricing strategies.

For renters navigating London’s competitive market, these trends underscore the importance of thorough research and careful budgeting. Meanwhile, landlords may wish to stay informed about legislative changes and market dynamics to make informed decisions about their rental properties.

item.title: landlord Law Newsround #448
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The start of August has brought a wave of housing-related news, with one particular issue standing out: the challenges renters face when charging electric vehicles (EVs). A recent survey highlights that tenants often encounter significant hurdles in accessing EV charging facilities, raising questions about fairness and accessibility in the rental market.

EV Charging Challenges for Renters

The survey reveals that renters are at a distinct disadvantage compared to homeowners when it comes to charging their EVs. Homeowners typically have the freedom to install charging points on their property, whilst renters must navigate complex negotiations with landlords or property management companies. This disparity could hinder the adoption of electric vehicles among tenants, especially as the UK moves towards greener transport solutions.

For landlords, this presents an opportunity to adapt to changing tenant needs. Installing EV charging points could make rental properties more appealing, particularly in urban areas where EV usage is on the rise. However, the costs and logistical challenges involved may deter some landlords from taking this step.

The Broader Implications for the Rental Market

This issue underscores a broader trend in the housing market: the growing expectation for rental properties to meet modern lifestyle demands. As EVs become more common, tenants are increasingly prioritising properties with charging facilities. Landlords who fail to address this demand risk losing out to competitors who are more forward-thinking.

Additionally, policymakers may need to consider measures to encourage landlords to invest in EV infrastructure. This could include incentives such as tax reliefs or grants, making it more financially viable for landlords to install charging points. Without such support, the gap between homeowners and renters in accessing EV facilities could widen further.

It’s worth noting that this issue also ties into the UK’s broader environmental goals. With the government aiming to phase out petrol and diesel cars by 2030, ensuring equitable access to EV charging is crucial. Renters, who make up a significant portion of the population, must not be left behind in this transition.

What This Means for Borrowers and Investors

For those considering property investment, the demand for EV-friendly rentals could influence future decisions. Properties with charging facilities may attract tenants more easily and command higher rents, potentially offering better returns for investors. Meanwhile, borrowers looking to purchase a rental property might factor in the cost of installing EV charging points when calculating their budget.

As the housing market continues to evolve, staying attuned to these trends could prove beneficial for both landlords and tenants. The growing importance of EV charging facilities is just one example of how shifting priorities are reshaping the rental landscape.

In conclusion, the challenges faced by renters in accessing EV charging facilities highlight a pressing issue in the housing market. Addressing this disparity will require collaboration between landlords, policymakers, and tenants to ensure a fair and sustainable approach to greener transport solutions.

item.title: Tenancy fraud poses £4.1bn risk to rental sector
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK’s private rental sector faces a staggering £4.1bn annual risk due to fraudulent tenancy applications, according to recent analysis by Goodlord. Examining over one million tenant references, the research revealed that 41 applications per 1,000 were flagged for suspected fraud between July 2025 and June 2026. While this marks a slight decline from the peak of 46.6 per 1,000 in late 2024, suspected fraud remains significantly higher than historical levels.

Rising Fraud Rates and Regional Variations

Goodlord’s findings highlight a sharp 40% increase in suspected fraud cases in 2025 compared to the previous year. The company estimates the average financial impact of a fraudulent tenancy at £9,601, factoring in costs such as rent arrears, legal fees, property damage, and void periods. Applying this to the UK’s 5.3 million privately rented households, assuming two tenant references per property, the potential annual exposure could reach £4.1bn.

Regional discrepancies were also evident, with London recording fraud rates nearly double the national average. The West Midlands and the North West followed closely, while overseas applications also showed higher-than-average fraud rates. Notably, properties with monthly rents exceeding £10,000 saw fraud rates nearing 18 per 1,000 applications, significantly higher than those in more affordable rental markets.

Evolving Fraud Tactics

The analysis of confirmed fraud cases in 2025 revealed a worrying trend: fake employment references surged by 226.6% year-on-year, becoming the fastest-growing category of fraud. Referee fraud and identity manipulation also saw substantial increases, rising by 146.4% and 140.4%, respectively. While these categories have slightly declined in 2026, they remain above 2024 levels.

Nishma Parekh, director of referencing at Goodlord, emphasised the growing sophistication of fraudsters. “Fraudsters are no longer relying on a single forged payslip – they’re building entire fake identities, complete with false employers and invented referees,” she explained. “The industry needs to shift from spotting individual red flags to identifying patterns throughout the referencing process.”

Parekh also stressed the importance of consistent reviews to stay ahead of evolving fraud tactics. As fraudsters continue to refine their methods, landlords and letting agents may wish to adopt more robust verification processes to mitigate risks.

Protecting the Rental Sector

With fraud posing a multi-billion-pound threat to the rental sector, stakeholders could benefit from enhanced referencing systems and greater vigilance. Implementing advanced checks, such as cross-referencing employment details and verifying referee identities, might help reduce the risk of fraudulent applications.

For landlords, staying informed about emerging fraud trends and investing in reliable referencing services could prove essential in safeguarding their properties and finances. As the rental market evolves, proactive measures may be key to maintaining trust and security for all parties involved.

Examining over one million tenant references, the research revealed that 41 applications per 1,000 were flagged for suspected fraud between July 2025 and June 2026. While this marks a slight decline from the peak of 46.6 per 1,000 in late 2024, suspected fraud remains significantly higher than historical levels.

Rising Fraud Rates and Regional Variations

Goodlord’s findings highlight a sharp 40% increase in suspected fraud cases in 2025 compared to the previous year. The company estimates the average financial impact of a fraudulent tenancy at £9,601, factoring in costs such as rent arrears, legal fees, property damage, and void periods. Applying this to the UK’s 5.3 million privately rented households, assuming two tenant references per property, the potential annual exposure could reach £4.1bn.

Regional discrepancies were also evident, with London recording fraud rates nearly double the national average. The West Midlands and the North West followed closely, while overseas applications also showed higher-than-average fraud rates. Notably, properties with monthly rents exceeding £10,000 saw fraud rates nearing 18 per 1,000 applications, significantly higher than those in more affordable rental markets.

Evolving Fraud Tactics

The analysis of confirmed fraud cases in 2025 revealed a worrying trend: fake employment references surged by 226.6% year-on-year, becoming the fastest-growing category of fraud. Referee fraud and identity manipulation also saw substantial increases, rising by 146.4% and 140.4%, respectively. While these categories have slightly declined in 2026, they remain above 2024 levels.

Nishma Parekh, director of referencing at Goodlord, emphasised the growing sophistication of fraudsters. “Fraudsters are no longer relying on a single forged payslip – they’re building entire fake identities, complete with false employers and invented referees,” she explained. “The industry needs to shift from spotting individual red flags to identifying patterns throughout the referencing process.”

Parekh also stressed the importance of consistent reviews to stay ahead of evolving fraud tactics. As fraudsters continue to refine their methods, landlords and letting agents may wish to adopt more robust verification processes to mitigate risks.

Protecting the Rental Sector

With fraud posing a multi-billion-pound threat to the rental sector, stakeholders could benefit from enhanced referencing systems and greater vigilance. Implementing advanced checks, such as cross-referencing employment details and verifying referee identities, might help reduce the risk of fraudulent applications.

For landlords, staying informed about emerging fraud trends and investing in reliable referencing services could prove essential in safeguarding their properties and finances. As the rental market evolves, proactive measures may be key to maintaining trust and security for all parties involved.

item.title: Property giant combines three surveying brands into one
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Three established surveying brands have merged under a single identity as part of a strategic consolidation by property services group LRG. The newly formed MAP Chartered Surveyors combines the expertise of Stirling Ackroyd, MAP and Romans, creating a national operation with over two centuries of combined industry experience.

A unified surveying proposition

The rebrand, which took effect in early July, brings together 50 surveyors operating across regional networks throughout England. The merger pools the resources of three respected firms: 150-year-old Stirling Ackroyd, 40-year-old MAP and 35-year-old Romans. Homeowners and lenders may find the consolidated service offers greater consistency in valuation and surveying standards nationwide.

Ryan Mathews, LRG's group managing director of surveying, explained: "This unification builds on each brand's longstanding commitment to rigorous inspections and client-focused advice. While our scale increases - with over 20,000 annual inspections on £8.4bn of property - we retain the local knowledge that underpins quality surveying."

Expanding national coverage

The newly formed MAP Chartered Surveyors continues to serve over 400 business clients and 200 lenders, with LRG planning to extend its reach through its branch network. The group's recent acquisition of Northern Estate Agencies Group, adding 36 branches across northern England, is expected to generate additional surveying referrals in regions including West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester.

Neil Louth, LRG group executive director, emphasised: "Clients will benefit from the same experienced professionals delivering consistent service standards, now backed by national coverage and the resources of one of the UK's largest property services groups."

The existing management team remains unchanged following the rebrand, ensuring continuity for existing clients. For those requiring surveying services, the merger may present an opportunity to access a broader range of expertise while maintaining the personal approach associated with local providers.

item.title: Property group adds first dedicated commercial management brand
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

LRG has recently expanded its portfolio with the acquisition of CBGA Property Management, marking its first foray into dedicated commercial property management. Established in 1989, CBGA specialises in managing commercial properties across sectors such as office, industrial, retail, and leisure. The company will continue to operate under its existing name from its London and Birmingham offices, maintaining its client-focused approach.

A Strategic Addition to LRG’s Portfolio

The acquisition brings LRG an established commercial property management operation with a national client base and a UK-wide managed portfolio. CBGA’s services include property management, service charge administration, client reporting, property inspections, facilities management, health and safety compliance, and pre-purchase due diligence. This move aligns with LRG’s strategy to partner with businesses that have strong leadership teams and trusted client relationships.

Simon Worthington, Chief Strategy Officer at LRG, highlighted the value of the acquisition, stating: “CBGA Property Management is an excellent business with an experienced team, a strong national portfolio, and long-standing client relationships. Its specialist expertise in commercial property management and client accounting makes it a valuable addition to LRG.” He also confirmed that CBGA will continue to operate under its existing name, with the same management team and partner-led service.

Focus on Continuity and Growth

For CBGA’s clients and team, the acquisition ensures continuity. Richard Turner, Partner at CBGA Property Management, emphasised the importance of finding a long-term partner that recognises the strength of their existing team and client relationships. He said: “LRG shares our focus on delivering a high-quality service and brings the scale and investment to support our continued development.”

This acquisition not only strengthens LRG’s position in the commercial property market but also provides a platform for future growth. Worthington added: “As our first dedicated commercial management brand, CBGA gives us a strong foundation from which to develop our wider commercial offering.”

LRG’s strategy focuses on sustainable growth, partnering with businesses that have clear opportunities for expansion. With CBGA’s existing management team remaining in place, LRG aims to build on its newly acquired expertise to enhance its commercial property services.

This move signifies a significant step for LRG as it diversifies its portfolio and strengthens its presence in the commercial property sector.

item.title: Rightmove reveals Brit buyers’ overseas property hotspots
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

For the second year running, Portugal's Algarve has emerged as the most sought-after overseas property destination for British buyers, according to Rightmove's latest analysis. The sunny coastal region maintained its top spot ahead of Paphos in Cyprus and Spain's Mallorca, rounding out a podium of perennial favourites. The ranking highlights British homeowners' enduring attraction to Mediterranean climates and relaxed lifestyles when considering properties abroad.

Mediterranean destinations dominate wish lists

Rightmove's data reveals a clear preference for sun-drenched European locations, with Spain claiming four spots in the top ten destinations. Following the Algarve, Paphos and Mallorca, France's Dordogne region took fourth place, while Spanish hotspots Alicante and Costa del Sol completed the top six. Greek islands Crete and Corfu ranked seventh and eighth respectively, with Murcia in Spain and Normandy in France rounding out the list.

At country level, Spain led the search rankings, followed by France and Italy - a trio that collectively accounts for the majority of British overseas property interest. Cyprus, Portugal and Greece filled the next three positions, with Malta, Ireland, Bulgaria and Gibraltar completing the top ten most searched nations.

Beyond holiday dreams: practical considerations

While summer browsing might begin with idyllic visions of overseas living, property professionals emphasise the importance of thorough research before committing to a purchase. NAEA Propertymark president Ian Harris notes that whilst warmer climates and lifestyle changes remain key motivators, practical considerations should form the foundation of any overseas property decision.

Prospective buyers might consider several crucial factors before taking the plunge:

  • Local property laws and ownership regulations
  • Taxation implications in both the UK and destination country
  • Residency requirements and visa restrictions
  • Ongoing maintenance and ownership costs
  • Access to healthcare and other essential services

Rightmove's overseas director Nick Robertson observes that summer holidays often serve as a research period for serious buyers: "Many use their break to explore locations properly, from assessing available property types to understanding what daily life would entail beyond the holiday atmosphere."

For those contemplating an overseas purchase, consulting regulated property professionals with local expertise could help navigate the complexities of international transactions. As the data shows, whilst the allure of Mediterranean living remains strong, informed decisions tend to yield the most successful outcomes for British buyers seeking properties abroad.

item.title: Landlords turn out in force for Renters’ Rights Act online briefing
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Over 100 landlords from Essex and Suffolk recently attended an online briefing about the Renters’ Rights Act, highlighting growing concerns about adapting to the legislation’s new requirements. The webinar, organised by estate agency Boydens, addressed key changes affecting the private rental sector, with particular focus on compliance challenges for property investors.

Key concerns for landlords under new legislation

The virtual event covered several major reforms introduced by the act, including the shift to periodic tenancies, the removal of Section 21 ‘no-fault’ evictions, and new rules governing rent increases and bidding practices. Attendees reportedly expressed significant apprehension about navigating the updated possession process when dealing with problematic tenancies.

Insurance solutions emerged as a key discussion point, with landlords exploring products that could protect against lost rental income, legal expenses and lengthy court proceedings. The high attendance figures – unusual for this period – suggest many property owners are actively seeking guidance on implementing the changes.

Growing demand for professional support

Boydens reported a surge in requests for assistance from landlords across their Essex and Suffolk branches, with compliance support becoming a priority for many investors. The agency’s landlord teams have reportedly seen unprecedented workloads as clients adapt to the new regulatory environment.

Philip Boyden, managing director at Boydens, commented: “The level of engagement demonstrates how seriously landlords are taking these reforms. While the sector remains profitable for well-prepared investors, many are understandably concerned about meeting their expanded obligations, particularly regarding property repossession procedures.”

The briefing also covered practical steps landlords might take to safeguard their investments, including reviewing insurance policies and updating tenancy management processes. With the Renters’ Rights Act introducing fundamental changes to landlord-tenant relationships, professional advice could prove valuable for those navigating the transition.

For landlords seeking to understand their new responsibilities, specialist lettings agencies and legal advisers may offer tailored support to help maintain compliant and profitable rental portfolios.
